hints.title: Two roots need not mean degree two
hints.body: A polynomial can also contain a factor with no real zeros, such as x2+1/4.
hints.recap: The real zero set does not determine the degree.
hints.pitfall: Extra turns need not introduce extra real roots.
hints.pause: Construct an allowed polynomial and differentiate it to test statement 1.

recall.reminder: The real zero set does not determine the degree.

hints.title: Check the sign of the integrand
hints.body: Try a polynomial with zeros at −1 and 1 that is negative between them; compare its signed integral with geometric area.
hints.recap: An integral keeps signs, whereas geometric area is nonnegative.
hints.pitfall: Symmetric zeros alone do not establish an even graph.
hints.pause: Use your example to test whether the area assertion must hold.

recall.reminder: An integral keeps signs, whereas geometric area is nonnegative.

hints.title: Track zeros through the two reflections
hints.body: −f(−x)=0 exactly when f(−x)=0. The input −x must therefore be one of the two original roots.
hints.recap: An outside sign does not move zeros; input reflection negates them.
hints.pitfall: You must also check that the transformation cannot create additional zeros.
hints.pause: Map both roots and select the statements that must hold.

recall.reminder: Treat input and output transformations separately.

solution:
Statement 1 need not hold. For p=1 and f(x)=(x2−1)(x2+14), the only real roots are ±1, but f′(x)=4x3−32x vanishes at 0 and ±3/8, all between them.

Statement 2 fails for f(x)=x2−1: 2∫01f(x)dx=−4/3, whereas the area is positive.

Statement 3 is guaranteed because −f(−x)=0 exactly when −x=±p, giving the same two roots x=±p. Only 3: answer D.
knowledgePattern: Distinguish guaranteed root transformations from shape assumptions
